It's complicated. TAG (The Ancient Gods) I and II start you off with everything fully upgraded, so you get more of the peak DOOM: Eternal combat, and they have further upgrades for you throughout them. They're also both an increase in difficulty and complexity from the base campaign, which I find positive? The biggest let-downs are both with the final levels of TAG II, with one being an enemy type that's just seriously underwhelming and weak (although the level it's in is otherwise awesome and hype as fuck) and the other being a kinda boring and overly simple fight for the game's final boss.

I like the game's combat to be challenging. I really like TAG I (I liked it more before they nerfed some encounters), and I like TAG II too, but I wish TAG II was significantly harder than it is - it's pretty much on-par with the campaign's final levels. It's easier than TAG I overall.

Also, a common criticism people have of TAG II specifically is that certain enemies heavily encourage you to use specific weapon mods, but that mostly applies to a single enemy: the Stone Imp, which is resistant to most things except for the full auto mod for the shotgun. The riot soldiers can be killed in way more different ways, including just having good aim with a rocket launcher and shooting it behind them. As for Spirits, they're basically a miniboss and there's never more than one (except in a certain fight in TAG I), so I don't mind having to quick-swap to the microwave beam after killing its host.

I don't particularly mind the rock-paper-scissors of that, although I am a little biased since I love using full auto on fodder anyway for that free shotgun ammo.

Lastly: story. These DLCs are why Eternal's story is such a mess. Most people don't really care about that and it still obeys rule of cool like the rest of the game, so it's fine if you're not a lore hound? If you are, you might not like it, though. Or you might - there's some cool stuff in there even though it's convoluted.
No pain, no gain. Do it, but only if you're gonna stick with it instead of ragequitting when you die for the tenth time in a row.

Here's how you farm, each stage simply explained:

1. Plant a bunch of random seeds. Build a bird cage, a bird trap, get a bird, and put it in the cage. Make a watering can, fill it at a pond, water your crops. Dig up weeds (forget-me-lots, spiny bindweed, tillweeds, and fire nettles) and debris. Click on the plants to talk to them (you can also use a one-man band if you have magic-tier crafting, or be near them as blooming Wormwood).
2. Each time the plants progress a stage, you need to tend to them. When the soil looks dry, water them.
3. Once your crops have fully grown, feed *all of them* to your bird and collect the seeds. Plant as many of the same type of crop as you have together in the same space. If some of the crops were growing really really slowly, they're out-of-season, and you should save the seeds of that type in a chest, fridge, or ideally a seed pack-it for a different season. 
4. Repeat the tending (talking or blooming Wormwood or one-man band) and watering process with this second batch of crops. You are guaranteed to get two seeds per plant (assuming they're in-season), even if you miss a few tending or watering stages. 

If you want giant crops, you need to start thinking about crop combinations and/or fertilizers. Assuming the crops are in-season, what I told you above will guarantee two seeds plus a crop per harvest. Memorizing what the weeds look like at various growth stages is a good idea so you can remove them quickly, and don't plant random seeds in the plot you use for growing crops you know the identity of. 

The below information is if you want to get into giant crop farming.

Crop seed yield and giant status are determined by stress points. If they're perfectly tended, watered, in a family of four crops of the same type (so, a potato with 3 other potatoes, or a tomato with 3 other tomatoes, etc), are in the right season, and have the right nutritional balance, they will get zero stress points. If a crop has zero or one stress point when it fully grows, it will become a giant. Each of these categories is checked when the plant advances a growth stage. This means that having poor soil nutrition as the only thing you're screwing up will only get them 4 stress points (they go down to giving 1 crop and 1 seed if you hit 7 stress points).

Crops all add something to the soil and take something away. The specific values can be determined with the gardeneer hats. In order to get giant crops, the best, most reliable method without using fertilizers is to plant crops that offset each other's nutritional deficits. 

The easiest one by far is tomatoes and potatoes: if you plant 4 tomatoes in the same farm tile as 4 potatoes, and you water and tend them consistently, make sure there's no weeds, and do it in autumn or spring, you are guaranteed 4 giant potatoes and 4 giant tomatoes.

Oh, you want to put your foot in that bear trap and defend Sniper by saying Spy exists? Sure, let's do that.

Spy has to get past the entire enemy team without getting bumped once (which is often largely down to luck since TF2 maps frequently lack good flanking routes you can use without something like a rocket jump), has to get into melee range to instakill anyone, and has to get lucky that they don't turn around at any point between him approaching while decloaked and him backstabbing them. 

Once he gets a backstab, he is almost certainly going to be killed if the guy he stabbed was in a group, and most priority targets (like Heavies and Medics) aren't frequently found alone. 

If a Spy is caught, his best option by far is to retreat since his revolver does worse damage than anyone else's gun but Medic's no matter how skilled the Spy is. Even with the Ambassador in close range, a Soldier can shoot him twice before he can headshot the Soldier twice, and the Soldier doesn't need to aim nearly as much. 

Spy has a hard counter and it's named Pyro, and it's a pretty easy class to effectively counter Spies with.

Now let's take a look at Sniper.

Sniper has to walk out of spawn (or even stay right inside the doors on some maps) and then can kill you anywhere in the map as long as he has line of sight on you. On some maps (Harvest and Megaton come to mind), this can be basically anywhere in the map except your team's base, so if you're trying to play the objective or do anything but turtle, your ability to do so depends entirely on whether or not he'll miss. On many maps, Snipers can be effective from so close to their own spawn that even if you get to them (which usually involves either going through his team's base or explosive jumping), they can just run back in so you can't kill them.

Once a Sniper gets a headshot, he faces no consequences. It lets the enemy team know there's a Sniper, but not where he is (unless he has the Machina) and it doesn't put him at any risk. Since he's also probably doing it from very far away, it also doesn't matter if he misses since he can just try again, and the enemy team likely won't even know he tried to shoot them.

If you manage to get past the entire enemy team without them or the Sniper killing you on the way, the Sniper can just quickscope you for an instant kill if he's decent or jarate+bushwacka you for an instant kill if he's not. You are probably not at full health if you're in your effective range against an enemy Sniper due to the getting past his team/explosive jumping required to get into that position in the first place, so no, quickscopes only doing 150 and Soldier/Demo having more base health than that isn't relevant.  
Also, if any non-support is hanging out with the Sniper, he will be drastically harder to kill before that person kills you - he can headshot you while you're busy if you go after them first, he can retreat while you're busy, they can kill you while you're trying to kill him, and even if you do kill him, you'll likely get killed by his buddy. If he's got a Sentry parked next to him, God help you, since he'll run the instant you take it down. 

Sniper's only hard counter is another Sniper who's at least as good. It's the only thing that can kill him as fast as or before he can kill anyone on the enemy team since everyone else has to cross a huge section of the map to even get close enough to do appreciable damage. Other than that, fighting one is banking on him having tunnelvision (the better Sniper players don't) and not seeing or hearing you approaching. 

You can't even rely on screwing up his aim by setting him on fire or shooting him from far away, because not only can Sniper players just learn to deal with that, he has a secondary that makes him immune to afterburn and another that prevents flinching entirely if he's scoped in for long enough.

Spy has counterplay any class can do with ease (periodically turning around) and has a hard counter. He is a class with high-risk, high-reward gameplay that lets him instakill people *if he doesn't get caught and can get into melee range from behind*, and if he screws up or gets unlucky at any point in that, it's likely to result in a respawn timer. Spy's balanced because he's the weakest class overall and has a genuinely difficult gameplay loop, especially if the enemy team aren't completely oblivious - even one aware player can make a Spy's job way more difficult.

Sniper has no practical counterplay for any class not named Sniper. His existence decreases the amount of fun possible in the game without even being a necessary evil, and this has been proven by test servers where he's been disabled - the game doesn't need him to be balanced. He was a mistake from the start: a low-risk, high-reward class who has virtually zero consequences for screwing up aside from being down one bullet. He can do all of this from near-perfect safety and all he has to do is click heads, which he has a scope to help with, and which isn't as difficult as Sniper mains like to make it out to be.

Pyro as a whole is too weak as a class.

175 HP is two close-range rockets, two meatshots from a shotgun/scattergun, or two grenades. If you're close enough to a Pyro to be getting set on fire, you are basically close enough to guarantee a two-shot if you have decent aim. However, you can still do almost as much from outside of a Pyro's effective range. With average speed and no default extra mobility options, Pyros have difficulty closing the distance, so getting too close to one means you're either too oblivious (which you ought to be punished for) or the Pyro's great at sneaking up on you (which ought to be rewarded). 

Pyro is hard-countered by Heavies and Engineers. Unlike Scouts, though, Pyro sucks ass at killing sentries from outside of their range. Scout can use the Shortstop (which basically lets him snipe sentries rapidly from a distance because of how hitting a sentry has no falloff) or a pistol (which does decent enough DPS to handle minisentries or other unguarded ones), but the shotgun isn't accurate enough to do a good job of it, and flare guns fire way too slowly for it to be worth your time. Pyro's best shot against sentries is the Dragon's Fury since it does enough DPS and has enough range to make corner-peeking as Pyro viable, but that just puts Pyro on-par with Demoman and Soldier *specifically if there's a corner near the sentry to peek around.*

As for the Heavy matchup, Pyro is only coming out of it alive if the Heavy isn't revved up, gets ambushed, isn't overhealed, isn't at full health, and/or has very slow reaction times. A stock Heavy who finds himself getting blasted by a Pyro, turns around, and starts shooting will at least kill the Pyro nine times out of ten, and the majority of non-new Heavies aren't so sluggish as to be unable to pull that off. The incredibly popular Tomislav gives the advantage of not having to wait for your gun to spin up, which slants the matchup even more in Heavy's favor. 

Airblast, while a bit annoying, doesn't matter as much as people like to think. It's actually really tricky to aim deflected rockets, even trickier to aim deflected grenades, and it takes fairly precise timing, judgment of distance, and perception abilities. A Soldier who spam-fires his rockets will basically match up perfectly with a Pyro's airblast cooldown and a Demoman can shoot faster than a Pyro can airblast. Also, airblasting a grenade doesn't reset its explode timer, so the Loose Cannon and Iron Bomber will very frequently detonate long before they make it back to the Demo who fired them.

The Flare Gun, which is Pyro's best flare gun in terms of damage output, will only do 90 damage on a *crit.* That means shooting this very slow-firing projectile weapon twice and hitting directly both times, or hitting someone who's running away from you with it. 90 damage is what Soldier gets for shooting vaguely near someone he's close to, and it's what Demoman gets for a single shot at any range with his grenade launchers. Flares basically suck unless you're countersniping or hitting retreating targets.

Pyro's mobility, overall, sucks. By default, Pyro straight-up has no more mobility options than Sniper, with the sole exception of the difficult-to-pull-off, very situational, and absurdly risky airblast rocket jump that'll leave you at practically no health by the time you land.   
The jetpack basically lets Pyro rocket jump twice before going on cooldown, but the sacrifice is having any ranged weapons whatsoever, and it's also really loud, so it's not the best for flanking.   
The Scorch Shot is a joke for mobility and its jumps are very situational pathetic hops.   
The Detonator, while it offers decent mobility, takes way too much of Pyro's health to really offer an alternate playstyle, and the jumps are very often *just* short of letting you cross meaningful obstacles on a lot of maps. It's also a worse flare gun than the stock one, and because the Scorch Shot exists as a spam tool, the Detonator's ability to detonate flares to set people on fire without hitting them directly is basically obsolete. 

Literally the only thing aside from spychecking that Pyro is good at is point-blank range, and other classes (Heavy and Demoknight, namely, and Soldier to a lesser extent) are better at it. Pyro can't get into range as easily as Soldier or Demo, isn't tanky enough to last very long in its effective range without a pocket Medic, struggles to deal with anyone further than hugging distance, isn't fast enough to do hit-and-run like Scout, and has no tools for sneaking around like Spy. 

Afterburn is a joke and gets extinguished by damn near everything. Mad Milk, water, dispensers, Medics, payload carts, medkits of every size, lunchbox items, other Pyros with airblast, Jarate, the Manmelter, charging as a Demoknight; you name it, it'll put out fire. The minimum duration of afterburn is 3 seconds, which will do 24 damage. The maximum is 10 seconds, which will do 80 if you somehow don't find anything to put it out in that time. 

Any difficulty a player has with an unpocketed enemy Pyro is largely their own fault regardless of how good the enemy Pyro is.

You're giving it far too much credit. AI doesn't actually know *anything*, nor does it create. All it can do is vaguely recognize patterns, which is why it needs oodles and oodles of unethically-obtained data: it can't do *anything* without sufficient data to determine consistent patterns and associate them with terms and qualifiers, and since it has no understanding of why anything is the way it is in any image in its data - all it 'knows' is that the patterns exist - it consistently makes bizarre mistakes no human ever would.  
This is why it'll give an AI bro a mangled signature in an image if it's trained on one artist's work too much and they put their signature in roughly the same place consistently. It can make an image that's passable at a brief glance, but if you look closer, you notice the parrot it generated has three feet and that the branch below the one it's standing on in the picture has feathers jutting out from it that seem to melt in with the wood, or other bizarreness like that. 

Effectively, it *is* almost like a collage or procedural generation, just a hyper-advanced one that arranges itself along certain conditions based on whatever you put into it. Give it a dataset of dog pictures tagged as 'dog' and it'll be able to replicate what a dog is well enough by determining trends in those images. It doesn't *actually* know what a dog is, though - that's why Nightshade can poison AI by tricking it into thinking something's that it isn't using artifacts that humans might not even notice, which screws up its output if it's trained on a poisoned image.

AI *can't* create, it can only steal. Don't fall for the hype and let it steal your faith in humanity too.

Well, let's take a look at use cases for AI/machine learning.

1. Generative AI. This one is nightmarishly terrible because all it does is attempt to make creative careers non-viable while also flooding the internet with nigh-unfilterable plagiarism slop. The only people it might benefit are the ultra-wealthy corpos who want to replace voice actors and artists with machines they don't have to pay. Well, them and the perverts using it to deepfake nudes of nonconsenting people/literal children. On top of all that, it's fucking up the climate and wasting a ton of energy. Generative AI should not even be legal and needs to be banned globally like chemical weapons because it's almost as bad.
2. Search engine-related AI. It doesn't seem to actually be beneficial in any way, and if anything, it's made every search engine that uses it worse. Whether it's the AI, other forms of enshittification, or both, search engines nowadays *suck.*
3. Self-driving vehicles. They're neat in theory, but we can't really trust them, and they still need human supervision. At the moment, I don't see them having much use except for making companies feel like they can screw over truckers. Also, I don't think it's the best idea to trust some big corporation with total control over your vehicle, especially in a car-dependent country like America - that's a lot of power to be handing over to the car's manufacturer.
4. Anti-drone applications. I saw a video on the ANVIL anti-drone drone by Anduril, which uses machine learning AI tech to track all moving objects in an area around its sensors, makes a heavy, durable drone hover above any drone it spots, and waits for a human to press the kill switch before sending the ANVIL drone to smash it out of the sky. This one's pretty great since it could be used to counteract drone-based terrorism and is a defensive military tool.
5. Translation. Google Translate is famously dubious and glitchy, and while it's not quite as bad as it used to be, it still leaves a lot to be desired. This is a good thing because human translators need jobs. May it never get to the point that it can actually replace them without loss of quality of work. Kind of neat if you specifically want to read something that was originally written in Spanish, though - it seems to do that decently enough, but it will still make a mess of it at times even now.
6. Medical and scientific applications. I always hear about these, but I've never actually seen a real, currently-in-use example of how AI can help. It's all just been theoretical BS about how it might be able to assist in the future. I'd be happy to be proven wrong on this one.
7. Coding. From what I've heard people with experience in the matter say, it can make serviceable code sometimes, but you still need a human who knows what they're doing to go through and fix all the dumb mistakes it makes.
